{"id": "a9bdf2fc-f8ab-4743-962e-12528c2d1612", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "No, this doesn't indicate an MTU misconfiguration — it's expected behavior from TCP segmentation offloading, not a sign your MTU is wrong.

**What's happening:**
- Your jumbo frame MTU of 9001 bytes is a wire-level limit — the actual Ethernet frames sent/received on the network never exceed that.
- `tcpdump` on Linux captures packets at the kernel's network stack *before* the NIC driver performs **TSO (TCP Segmentation Offload)** on egress, or *after* **GRO (Generic Receive Offload)** reassembles frames on ingress. Both are hardware/driver offload features that batch many wire-sized packets into one large "software" packet for efficiency — this is the pattern you're describing.
- So a single large "segment" tcpdump shows you (e.g., ~20,000 bytes) is really several real wire-level packets, each still capped at 9001 bytes of MTU, that the NIC driver either hasn't segmented yet (TSO, outbound) or already reassembled (GRO, inbound) by the time the capture point sees them.

**How to confirm this for yourself, if you want certainty:**
- Check offload settings: `ethtool -k <interface>` — look at `tcp-segmentation-offload`, `generic-receive-offload`, `large-receive-offload`.
- Capture with offload-aware filtering: Wireshark/tcpdump can show the "not-captured-length" or you can temporarily disable TSO/GRO (`ethtool -K <interface> tso off gro off`) and re-capture — you'd then see every segment clamped to 9001 bytes.
- Use VPC Traffic Mirroring instead of a local capture if you want to see traffic as it actually appears on the wire, unaffected by local offload reassembly.

So unless you disable offloads and still see >9001-byte segments on the wire, your MTU is fine — this is just an artifact of where tcpdump sits relative to the NIC's offload engine.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
